title: The Goofus style and the Goofus horn
summary: They discuss the Goofus style, its accenting, and the Goofus horn Hug owned.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: What was this Goofus style that they talked about? Goofus style?
Well, it's quite hard to explain it by talking about it, more or less than hearing it or playing it.
Are there any records that you think of as being typically Goofus?
Well, the Goofus Five was a perfect example of that style. I can't remember. I did have a couple of old records by the Goofus Five.
Would be the kind of the Red Nickels group?

Oh, the Red Nickels type. More, yeah. I would say that it leans very strong towards the Red Nickels type of record. They accented. They did like the . You know, they accented. It was a very strong accentuation. They're syncopated style but accenting. They didn't accent the second beat or they didn't the fourth beat as we do in the Strip-Dixieland type of music. It was more or less . I can't sing it as well as I could play it. In those days, if I had a piano here, I could give an example of the accentuation that they used. It was a very, very peculiar style of playing. I say that the Chicago style of music kind of revolved around that quite a bit.
Well, we'll get to a piano or something. You can give me a couple of bars and some of these different things.

You can demonstrate it a lot better than just by humming it. But that was a good point that you brought out because the Goofus style of music was really a very weird, weird style. I think they used that bariton sax, or the bass sax rather, played a very important part in there. And they used to use a little horn called the Goofus horn. Do you remember that thing?
Yeah, I've heard it on the record.

I owned one of those at one time. It was made just like the keys were set up just like a keyboard with little round buttons, you know, that you pressed. And they had a long rubber tube that you blew into. And you could get a sound sort of like a harmonica out of it. And you could really play some real crazy things on it.

Yeah, I used to use it. I used it quite a bit when I was playing with Eddie Miller and Bill Padron back in the early 19, in 29, 30. We used to use it quite a lot. In fact, if I dig up one right now and make a record of it, it's a novelty, you know. They have one in the Cabildo.

That's a true, a lot there. What bands played Goofus style in down here? I can't say that I can remember any of the New Orleans bands playing that style. It wasn't too influential. I don't think it was too influential.
I don't think it went over too big with the New Orleans bands down here. I think that was used mostly by the bands up north, you know.
